templates.title: Ad frequency caps — impressions served over the cap
templates.subtopic: rolling time windows, LAG with an offset, tie-breaking

sections.scenario: Ad platforms let advertisers on some campaign types cap how often one person sees a campaign: at most N impressions in a rolling window of hours or days. Delivery enforces the cap from counters that can lag behind the impression log, so an audit job measures over-delivery after the fact from the log itself. Advertisers are not charged for over-cap impressions in this hypothetical policy, so the count has to be exact.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns campaign_id, impressions, over_cap_impressions, users_over_cap for every campaign in campaigns, ordered by campaign_id. Order a user's impressions of one campaign by served_at, then impression_id. An impression is over the cap when the number of that user's impressions of that campaign served in the half-open window (served_at − window_hours, served_at] and not after it in that order (so itself included) is greater than the campaign's frequency_cap. impressions counts the campaign's impressions, over_cap_impressions those over the cap, and users_over_cap the distinct users with at least one. {{cap_rule}} {{log_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). The sample has {{impressions}} logged rows; production has billions of impressions a day, so a self-join per user and campaign is acceptable here but its cost should be discussed.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical caps, windows and traffic. Over-cap impressions were still served and still count toward the window of later impressions: the audit measures exposure, not what delivery intended.
sections.criteria: Correct half-open window and strict cap comparison; deterministic tie-breaking by impression_id; over-cap impressions still counted in later windows; campaigns with no impressions reported; at the Very Hard level, per-campaign windows, one row per impression and invalid traffic excluded. Explains the cost of the chosen approach at production volume.

clarifications.q: Is an impression exactly window_hours older still inside the window?
clarifications.a: No. The window is (served_at − window_hours, served_at]: one exactly a window earlier has left it.

clarifications.q: With a cap of 3, is the third impression over the cap?
clarifications.a: No. The cap is the number allowed; the fourth in a window is the first over it.

clarifications.q: Two impressions in the same second?
clarifications.a: Order them by impression_id; the smaller id was served first, so only the later one can be the one that crosses the cap.

clarifications.q: Does an over-cap impression count toward the window of the next one?
clarifications.a: Yes. It was shown, so the person saw it.

clarifications.q: Campaigns with no impressions?
clarifications.a: Report them with zeros.

hints: Clean the log first (one row per impression, valid rows only, where the level needs it), then join the campaign's cap and window.

Because a user's impressions are in a total order, the window ending at an impression is a contiguous run that ends at it. The impression is over the cap exactly when the impression frequency_cap places earlier is still inside its window.
LAG(served_at, frequency_cap) reads that impression directly. A window frame with RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL … PRECEDING cannot take a per-campaign interval, and it treats same-second rows as peers.
followups: The audit must refund over-cap impressions in near real time instead of nightly. What state per (user, campaign) do you keep, and how big is it?
Delivery enforces caps from a counter replicated across regions with a few seconds of lag. Estimate the over-delivery that lag allows and how you would bound it.
The cap moves from "per campaign" to "per advertiser across all its campaigns". What changes in the query and in the state you keep?
Impressions arrive up to six hours late. Which flags computed yesterday can change, and how do you recompute only those?

rules.ask: With a 7-day window and a user who sees thousands of impressions a week, what does the self-join cost, and what would you do instead?
Two impressions share a served_at. What count does a RANGE frame give each of them, and which one is really over the cap?
Prove that comparing with the impression frequency_cap places earlier is equivalent to counting the window.
The client and server copies of an impression disagree on served_at by a second. Which do you keep, and could the choice flip a flag?

templates.title: Conversion lift study — test versus holdout readout
templates.subtopic: experiment readout, deduplication, conditional aggregation

sections.scenario: A conversion lift study measures what an ad campaign caused rather than what it was credited with: people are randomly assigned to a test cell, which can see the campaign's ads, or a holdout (control) cell, which cannot, and the conversion rates of the two cells are compared. Ad platforms describe this kind of study publicly. Conversions arrive from a browser pixel and, increasingly, from the advertiser's server; public documentation for sending both asks for a shared event ID so the copies can be deduplicated. You are writing the readout for {{studies}} studies.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns, for every study, study_id, test_users, test_converters, test_conversions, control_users, control_converters, control_conversions, lift, ordered by study_id. A conversion counts for a user in a study when its event_name equals the study's event_name and its time is at or after the user's assigned_at and before the study's ends_at. *_users counts the users in the cell, *_converters those with at least one counted conversion, *_conversions the counted conversions. lift = (test_rate − control_rate) / control_rate, where each rate is converters / users, as a double precision value; it is NULL when the control cell has no converters. {{dedup_rule}} {{assign_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). A user can be in several studies, and one conversion can count in each of them. Compute rates in floating point, not integer division.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical studies, users and events; no statistical significance is required here. Assignment happens at or after starts_at.
sections.criteria: Assignment and conversions reduced to the right grain before joining; users with no conversions kept; time window [assigned_at, ends_at) and the study's event only; deduplication on (event_name, event_id) with the earliest copy's time; at the Very Hard level, duplicate assignments collapsed and contaminated users excluded; lift NULL when undefined and computed in floating point.

clarifications.q: Does a conversion before the user was assigned count?
clarifications.a: No. The user was not in the study yet. One exactly at assigned_at does count.

clarifications.q: Is ends_at inclusive?
clarifications.a: No. The window is [assigned_at, ends_at).

clarifications.q: Do other event types count, for example AddToCart in a Purchase study?
clarifications.a: No. Only the study's event_name.

clarifications.q: What identifies one conversion?
clarifications.a: The pair (event_name, event_id). Copies with the same pair are one conversion; its time is the earliest copy.

clarifications.q: How should lift be returned when the control cell has no converters?
clarifications.a: NULL; it is undefined, not zero or infinite.

hints: Reduce each input to its grain first: one row per (study, user) for assignments, one row per (event_name, event_id) for conversions.
Count per (study, user) with a LEFT JOIN, so users with no conversions still count as users, then aggregate per study with COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE …).
Cast before dividing: test_converters::float8 / test_users.
followups: Add a 95% confidence interval for the difference in conversion rates. What do you compute per cell, and when does the normal approximation stop being reasonable?
The holdout is 10% of users and the study runs for weeks. How would you make the daily readout incremental instead of recomputing from raw events?
Some conversions are reported only by the server, days late. How does that bias a readout taken while the study is running, and in which direction?
A user is assigned on one device and converts on another while logged out. What does that do to the measured lift, and what can the data model do about it?

rules.ask: A test user with no conversions: does your join keep them in test_users? Show where.
Is event_id alone a safe deduplication key, or can two different events share one?
Would averaging per-user conversion flags give the same rate as converters / users? What about averaging per-day rates?
Where exactly would integer division have silently produced 0 in your query?

templates.title: Group message delivery receipts — messages slower than the SLA
templates.subtopic: interval membership joins, relational division, outer joins

sections.scenario: A messaging app with end-to-end encryption never sees message content, but delivery metadata — which message, which recipient, when a delivered or read receipt came back — is what reliability teams can measure. A message to a group is only fully delivered when every member who should receive it has a device that acknowledged it. The reliability dashboard needs the messages sent between {{start}} and {{end}} that took longer than {{sla}} seconds to reach every recipient, or have not reached all of them.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns message_id, chat_id, recipients, delivered_recipients, delivery_seconds for messages with sent_at in [{{start}}, {{end}}), ordered by message_id. The recipients of a message are the chat's members at sent_at (joined_at <= sent_at and left_at NULL or later than sent_at), other than the sender. A recipient's delivery time is their earliest receipt of either type. delivered_recipients counts recipients with at least one receipt; delivery_seconds is the time from sent_at to the last recipient's delivery when all recipients have one, else NULL. Return only messages that have at least one recipient and either are not fully delivered or took more than {{sla}} seconds. {{member_rule}} {{receipt_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). The tables hold metadata only; there is no content column and none is needed. Production has hundreds of billions of receipts a day.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical chats, users and timings; device clocks are already corrected to UTC. A missing receipt means none had arrived when the extract was taken.
sections.criteria: Recipients from membership at sent_at with the boundary rules; the sender excluded; earliest receipt per recipient, reads included; missing receipts kept by an outer join and reported as incomplete; strict SLA and half-open window; at the Very Hard level, receipts from non-recipients ignored and messages with no recipients excluded. Discusses finality and privacy of delivery metadata sensibly.

clarifications.q: Is a member who joined at exactly sent_at a recipient?
clarifications.a: Yes: joined_at <= sent_at. A member whose left_at equals sent_at is not.

clarifications.q: Does a read receipt count as delivery?
clarifications.a: Yes. A message cannot be read before it is delivered, so a read is proof of delivery at that time.

clarifications.q: A recipient has three receipts. Which time is their delivery time?
clarifications.a: The earliest.

clarifications.q: Exactly {{sla}} seconds?
clarifications.a: Not slow. Only more than {{sla}} seconds is reported.

clarifications.q: Is the window end inclusive?
clarifications.a: No. A message sent exactly at {{end}} is outside it.

hints: Build the recipient set first: one row per (message, recipient) from an interval join of messages to memberships.
Collapse receipts to one earliest time per (message, recipient), then LEFT JOIN it to the recipient set so missing receipts stay visible as NULLs.
"Every recipient has a receipt" is COUNT(delivered_at) = COUNT(*) per message; the full delivery time is the MAX of the earliest times.
followups: Report the p50 and p99 of full delivery time per hour for groups of size 2, 3–10 and 11+. Where would you store the raw distribution to make that cheap?
A group has 1 000 members. Is "every recipient delivered" still the right reliability metric? Propose one that is not dominated by the slowest phone.
Receipts arrive for days (a phone off on holiday). When can a message's numbers be final, and how do you keep the dashboard both fresh and correct?
Privacy review asks that no table keep (sender, recipient, time) triples longer than needed. Which aggregates would you keep after 30 days, and what can no longer be answered?

rules.ask: A member left an hour after the message. Should they be a recipient, and does your join say so?
A recipient's second device acknowledged 10 minutes after the first. Which time measures delivery to that person?
A recipient whose phone is off has no receipt row. Where does your query count them?
What would double-count in your query if a member had two membership rows for one chat?

templates.title: "People you may know" — friend-of-friend suggestions
templates.subtopic: two-hop counting, heaps for top k

sections.scenario: Social networks suggest people you may know, and the most common public explanation of a suggestion is the number of mutual friends. Candidate generation for those suggestions starts from the friendship graph: the friends of a person's friends, scored by how many mutual friends they share, with people already connected or blocked removed. You are writing that candidate generator for a batch of users.
sections.problem: Implement suggest(edges, queries, k, blocked=(), hidden=frozenset(), min_mutual=1). edges is a list of undirected friendships (a, b). For each user u in queries, return a list of up to k pairs (v, mutual): candidates v who are not u and not already u's friends, where mutual is the number of users who are friends of both, and mutual >= min_mutual. Order by mutual descending, then v ascending. A user with no friends, or not in the graph, gets []. Return one list per query, in order. {{edge_rule}} {{block_rule}} {{hidden_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 300 000 edges, 40 000 users and 2 500 queries in one call. User ids are non-negative integers. Expected: build the graph once, then work proportional to the two-hop neighbourhood of each query user, never to the number of users.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical graph sizes. Real systems add many other signals; here the score is the mutual-friend count alone.
sections.criteria: Correct candidate set (no self, no friends, no blocked pairs in either order); mutual counts unaffected by duplicate, reversed or self edges; ordering and min_mutual boundary exact; at the Very Hard level, hidden users skipped as connectors but still suggestible; complexity proportional to the two-hop neighbourhood with a heap or partial sort for the top k.

clarifications.q: Can a current friend be suggested if they have many mutual friends?
clarifications.a: No. Existing friends and the user themself are never candidates.

clarifications.q: Ties on mutual friends?
clarifications.a: Smaller user id first.

clarifications.q: What if fewer than k candidates qualify?
clarifications.a: Return all of them.

clarifications.q: A user id in queries that never appears in edges?
clarifications.a: Return [] for it.

clarifications.q: Does blocking work in both directions?
clarifications.a: Yes. (a, b) in blocked means neither is suggested to the other.

hints: Build an adjacency map of sets once; sets make duplicate and reversed edges harmless and make "is v already a friend" O(1).
For a query user, walk friends of friends and count how often each candidate is reached: that count is the number of mutual friends.
You need only the best k of the counted candidates: heapq.nsmallest(k, ((-mutual, v), …)) avoids sorting all of them.
followups: One user has 5 000 friends and each of them has 5 000. What does a two-hop walk cost, and how would you cap or sample it?
Run this for every user every night on a graph with billions of edges. How would you express it as a distributed join, and where is the skew?
Rank by a weighted score that discounts mutual friends who have very many friends (an Adamic–Adar style weight). What changes in the counting?
A friendship is removed. Which users' suggestions can change, and how would you update them incrementally?

rules.ask: How many users does each query scan in the timing test, and how many does it need to?
You sort every candidate. How many are there for a well-connected user, and what does a heap of size k save?
How much memory does your adjacency map take for 300 000 edges, and what would you use for a billion?
Which key is hot in the two-hop self-join, and how do you salt or split it?

templates.title: Peak concurrent viewers of a creator's live broadcast
templates.subtopic: interval merging per key, sorting events

sections.scenario: Creators who go live see how many people are watching, and after the broadcast their insights show the peak. The player logs a session for every device that watches: when it started and when it stopped. People switch devices, lose connection and come back, and scroll past for a second, so a raw count of open sessions overstates the audience. You are computing the post-broadcast peak from the session log.
sections.problem: Implement peak_viewers(sessions, min_ms=0). sessions is a list of (viewer_id, start_ms, end_ms) with start_ms < end_ms, in any order; a session covers the half-open interval [start_ms, end_ms). Return (peak, first_ms, ms_at_peak): the largest number of distinct viewers watching at the same instant, the earliest time that number is reached, and the total time (summed over every stretch) during which exactly that many are watching. If no viewer counts, return (0, -1, 0). {{viewer_rule}} {{min_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 200 000 sessions over a two-hour broadcast (timestamps in milliseconds). Expected: O(n log n). Counting viewers separately at every boundary, or marking every millisecond, is far too slow.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical traffic. Session times are already on one clock.
sections.criteria: Correct half-open handling, with all events at one time applied before the count is read; viewers counted once via per-viewer merging of overlapping and touching sessions; min_ms applied after merging at the Very Hard level; correct first time and total time at the peak; O(n log n) with a clear argument.

clarifications.q: One viewer leaves at exactly the millisecond another joins. Were both watching at once?
clarifications.a: No. Intervals are half-open, so at that instant only the new viewer is watching.

clarifications.q: The same viewer on a phone and a laptop at once?
clarifications.a: At the Hard and Very Hard levels that can happen; they count once.

clarifications.q: What exactly is ms_at_peak?
clarifications.a: The total length of all stretches during which the count equals the peak, even if they are separated in time.

clarifications.q: What if sessions is empty?
clarifications.a: Return (0, -1, 0).

hints: Turn each counted interval into two events, +1 at its start and −1 at its end, sort them by time, and apply every event at the same time before reading the count.
The count after the events at time t holds until the next event time, which gives the length of each stretch.
To count a viewer once, first merge each viewer's sessions that overlap or touch; at the Very Hard level, apply min_ms to the merged intervals, not to raw sessions.
followups: Show the live count every second during the broadcast instead of after it. What state do you keep, and how do you handle a device that disappears without a stop event?
Sessions arrive from three regions with up to 30 seconds of delay. How do you publish a live number that does not jump backwards?
Ten thousand broadcasts are live at once and you need the top 100 by current viewers every second. What data structure, and what does each update cost?
You need the number of distinct viewers who watched at any point, for a broadcast with 50 million sessions, within 1%. What do you use, and what does it cost in memory?

rules.ask: At one timestamp a viewer leaves and another joins. In what order do your events apply, and does it matter for the peak?
Your merge treats touching sessions as one. What would change if a 1 ms gap also counted as continuous?
If the player only sent heartbeats every 10 seconds, what is the error bound on your peak?
Can a mergeable sketch answer the peak concurrent question, or only the distinct total? Why?

templates.title: Ad slots in a feed session — spacing, caps and advertiser alternation
templates.subtopic: interval spacing, layered DP, best-two-of-different-colour

sections.scenario: A social app's feed mixes organic posts with ads. For one scrolling session, a ranking system has already scored a candidate ad for every feed slot: the estimated value of showing that ad there, net of the estimated cost to the person's experience of displacing an organic post. A value can be negative. A hypothetical ad-load policy keeps ads apart so the feed does not feel like a catalogue. You are writing the routine that picks which slots get ads.
sections.problem: Implement best_ad_load(values, gap, max_ads=None, advertisers=None). values[i] is the integer net value of placing the candidate ad in slot i (slots are numbered in scrolling order from 0). Choose any set of slots such that any two chosen slots have at least gap organic slots between them: chosen slots p < q need q − p ≥ gap + 1. {{cap_rule}} {{advertiser_rule}} Return the largest possible total of the chosen values. Choosing no slots is allowed and gives 0.
sections.constraints: Up to 300 000 slots when there is no cap; up to 20 000 slots and max_ads ≤ 80 otherwise; gap ≥ 0; an empty feed is allowed; up to 500 distinct advertisers. Values are integers between −10⁶ and 10⁶. Expected: O(n) without a cap and O(n · max_ads) with one, independent of the number of advertisers.
sections.assumptions: Values, the spacing policy, the cap and the advertiser rule are hypothetical simplifications; real ad delivery also involves auctions, pacing and many other policies. Each slot has exactly one candidate ad, already chosen. The feed length is fixed for the session.
sections.criteria: Correct spacing (q − p ≥ gap + 1) and empty selection; O(n) DP without a cap and O(n · max_ads) layered DP with one, each layer reading only the previous; at Very Hard, an ending-at-slot state with the best two endings of different advertisers, and the insight that a negative ad can be worth placing as a separator; no recursion-depth failures; can reconstruct the selection and discuss an online version.

clarifications.q: Does gap count the organic slots between two ads, or the distance between them?
clarifications.a: The organic slots between them. With gap 2, ads in slots 3 and 6 are allowed (slots 4 and 5 are organic); slots 3 and 5 are not.

clarifications.q: Can I return an empty selection?
clarifications.a: Yes. If every value is negative or zero, the answer is 0.

clarifications.q: Is max_ads a maximum or an exact count?
clarifications.a: A maximum. Fewer ads are fine.

clarifications.q: With advertisers, may the same advertiser appear twice in the session?
clarifications.a: Yes, as long as some other advertiser's ad is shown between the two. Only ads that are next to each other in the chosen sequence must differ.

clarifications.q: Would the best answer ever include an ad with a negative value?
clarifications.a: Your algorithm should not assume it never does. Work out whether any rule makes it worthwhile.

clarifications.q: Do I need to return the chosen slots?
clarifications.a: Only the total. Reconstructing the slots is a follow-up.

hints: Without a cap: let best[i] be the best total using only slots before i. Either slot i − 1 is empty, or it holds an ad and the previous ad is at least gap + 1 slots earlier.
With a cap, add the number of ads to the state: best_j[i] is the best total using at most j ads in slots before i. Each layer reads only the previous one.

With advertisers, "best before slot i" is not enough: you need the best earlier selection whose last ad is from a different advertiser. Track the best ending, its advertiser, and the best ending from any other advertiser.
followups: Return the chosen slots as well. What do you store, and how do you choose among selections with the same total?
The feed is infinite: slots arrive as the person scrolls and you must decide each slot when it arrives. What does your offline answer become, and what would you measure to judge an online policy?
The policy changes to "at most max_ads ads in any window of 20 consecutive slots" instead of a session cap. How does the state change, and what does it cost?
Two different teams own the value model and the ad-load policy. How would you test that a policy change does not quietly shift value between advertisers?

rules.ask: Give a small feed where taking the single highest-value slot first loses, and say what your greedy misses.
How many valid selections does a 20 000-slot feed have, and what structure lets you avoid enumerating them?
Your inner loop scans earlier slots. What is the total work at 20 000 slots and 80 ads, and which running maximum removes that loop?
With 500 advertisers, what does taking the maximum over the other advertisers cost per slot? Do you need all of them?
What is the recursion depth for 300 000 slots in CPython, and how would you write it bottom-up?

templates.title: Degrees of separation on the friendship graph
templates.subtopic: bidirectional breadth-first search, shortest-path counting

sections.scenario: A social network stores friendships as an undirected graph. A product analytics team studies how closely people are connected — how many friendships separate two people — to understand how content can travel between communities. They have a snapshot of friendships and a list of pairs to measure, and they do not care about chains longer than a few steps.
sections.problem: Implement separation(friendships, queries, max_depth, inactive=None, count_paths=False). friendships is a list of (user_a, user_b) pairs of integer user ids; a friendship goes both ways and may appear more than once, in either order. For each (u, v) in queries, return the number of friendships on the shortest chain from u to v, or -1 if there is no chain of at most max_depth friendships. A user is 0 friendships from themselves, even a user who appears in no friendship. {{inactive_rule}} {{count_rule}} Return one answer per query, in query order.
sections.constraints: Up to 60 000 users with 300 000 friendship rows and 600 queries in the timing check (the graph can be larger in the follow-ups); 1 ≤ max_depth ≤ 6. A search that reaches most of the graph for every query is too slow; aim to touch only the neighbourhoods needed.
sections.assumptions: User ids, the snapshot and the queries are hypothetical. The output is a distance and a count, never a list of the people on a chain. The friendship list never contains a pair of a user with themselves.
sections.criteria: Correct undirected adjacency with repeated rows collapsed; inclusive max_depth; distance 0 for the same user; bidirectional search expanding whole layers from the smaller frontier, stopping at the first meeting layer; at Hard, deactivated accounts excluded from chains and endpoints; at Very Hard, correct shortest-chain counts (layer counts, products at the meeting layer); explains why each meeting user is equidistant; O(neighbourhoods touched) per query rather than O(graph).

clarifications.q: Is a friendship directed?
clarifications.a: No. If (a, b) is listed, a is b's friend and b is a's.

clarifications.q: Is max_depth inclusive?
clarifications.a: Yes. A chain of exactly max_depth friendships is reported; a longer one gives -1.

clarifications.q: What about a query for a user who appears in no friendship?
clarifications.a: That user has no friends: the answer is -1, unless the query asks for the distance from that user to themselves, which is 0.

clarifications.q: Does a repeated friendship row create a second chain?
clarifications.a: No. A chain is a sequence of distinct users; repeating a row changes nothing.

clarifications.q: Can I precompute all distances?
clarifications.a: Not for the graph sizes in the follow-ups: pairs grow with the square of the users.

hints: Run a breadth-first search from both ends at once and stop when the two searches meet. Each side only needs to go about half the distance.
Always grow the side whose current frontier is smaller. A frontier that includes a person with thousands of friends is expensive to expand.
Expand a whole layer at a time. When the new layer touches the other side's visited set, every touching user is the same distance from both ends.
For the count, carry the number of shortest ways to reach each user on each side; a meeting user contributes the product of the two.
followups: One user in the graph has 5 million friends (a public figure followed as a friend). How does that change your choice of which side to expand, and what does it do to the worst case?
The graph is 3 billion users and does not fit in one machine's memory. How would you answer the same batch of queries with a distributed engine, and how many rounds of data shuffling does it take?
Instead of exact distances for pairs, the team wants the average distance across the whole network. How would you estimate it without running a search from every user?
The snapshot is refreshed daily while the analysis runs for a week. What do you version, and how do you make the results reproducible?

rules.ask: From one end, how many users does your search touch before it reaches a user 5 friendships away when the average person has 10 friends?
Every friendship has the same weight. What does the heap buy you here, and what does it cost per step?
Does a depth-first search find the shortest chain first? How would you bound it, and what happens on a 60 000-user chain in CPython?
How much memory do all-pairs distances need for 60 000 users, and for 3 billion?
When counting shortest chains, a user can be reached twice in the same layer. Does your visited check drop the second way in?

templates.title: Debug the feed dwell-time calculator
templates.subtopic: interval reconstruction from client events, ordering, caps and thresholds

sections.scenario: A social app's feed measures how long each post was on screen. The app logs a start event when a post becomes visible enough to count and a stop event when it no longer is, plus a background event when the app leaves the screen. Events are uploaded in batches. A job turns one session's events into dwell time per impression, which feeds engagement metrics and ranking labels. After a client update that changed how uploads are batched, dwell times for some posts became implausibly long, posts glanced at for a moment started counting as viewed, and long reads were cut short. The function below is the suspect.
sections.problem:
Fix dwell_by_impression(events, min_visible_ms, cap_ms) so that it meets this specification. Each event is a dict {"imp", "kind", "ts"}: kind is "start", "stop" or "background" (whose imp is None), and ts is epoch milliseconds. {{upload_rule}}

  1. Order. Process events in ts order. At the same ts, stop and background events come before start events.
  2. Intervals. A start opens an interval for its impression; a start for an impression whose interval is already open is a repeat and changes nothing. A stop closes that impression's open interval (a stop with nothing open is ignored). A background closes every open interval at its ts. An interval still open after the last event closes at the largest ts in the list.
  3. Cap. Each interval contributes at most cap_ms: the cap applies to every interval separately, not to the impression's total.
  4. Viewable. An impression is viewable if at least one of its intervals lasted min_visible_ms or longer (before capping). Several short glances do not add up to a view.
  5. Output. {imp: dwell_ms} for viewable impressions only, where dwell_ms is the sum of that impression's capped intervals.
sections.constraints: Keep the function's shape and output format. Up to 200 000 events in a call; a sort plus one pass is expected. cap_ms ≥ min_visible_ms.
sections.assumptions: The event shape, the thresholds and every value are hypothetical, and the visibility rule that triggers start and stop is already applied on the device. Timestamps come from one device clock, so they are comparable within a session.
sections.criteria: Finds and explains every bug with its symptom (arrival order instead of time order; backgrounding closes only one post; a repeated start resets the interval; cap on the total instead of per interval; viewability judged on the total); sorts with the stop-before-start tie rule; fixes each minimally without new bugs; keeps a sort plus one pass; proposes a regression test per bug.

clarifications.q: Can two posts be visible at the same time?
clarifications.a: Yes. On a large screen, or while scrolling, two posts can each be visible enough to count.

clarifications.q: Why would the client send start twice for the same post?
clarifications.a: For example after a layout change while the post stays visible. It is a repeat; the interval keeps its original start.

clarifications.q: A stop and a start for the same post have the same ts. What happens?
clarifications.a: The stop first, so one interval ends and a new one begins. Both count separately.

clarifications.q: Is exactly min_visible_ms viewable?
clarifications.a: Yes. The comparison is inclusive.

clarifications.q: Does the cap apply before or after adding up intervals?
clarifications.a: Before: each interval is capped on its own.

clarifications.q: How many bugs are there?
clarifications.a: Several, of different kinds. Each has a test that only it fails.

hints: Feed the function the events of two upload batches with the later batch first. What does a stop that arrives before its start do?
Put two posts on screen and send the app to the background. How many intervals end?
Start a post, send start again 300 ms later, then stop it. What start time does the code use?
Write down an impression with two 0.6 × cap_ms intervals, and one with two intervals of half min_visible_ms. What should each produce?
followups: Write the smallest set of unit tests that would have caught every one of these bugs before the client update shipped.
The job moves into a streaming pipeline. When can you emit an impression's dwell, given that batches arrive late and out of order?
Device clocks jump (a user changes the time, or the phone syncs). How would you detect it in a session, and what would you do with the affected intervals?
The ranking team wants dwell as a label. Which of these bugs would have biased the label, in which direction, and for which kinds of posts?

rules.ask: Two events share a timestamp: a stop and a start for the same post. What does your sort key do with them, and what should happen?
Is only one post ever on screen? What does backgrounding the app do to the others?
The client repeats a start 300 ms after the first. Which start time should the interval keep, and what does your code keep?
An impression has two intervals of 0.6 × cap_ms. What dwell does the specification give, and what does your code give?
Five glances of 200 ms each: is that a view under the specification?

templates.title: Ad account reports in every advertiser's time zone
templates.subtopic: time-zone-aware rollups, restatement, late data, reconciliation with billing

sections.scenario: An advertising business serves about {{daily_impressions}} ad impressions a day for {{ad_accounts}} ad accounts. Each ad account has a reporting time zone and a currency, set when the account is created. Advertisers read reports in the ads manager and through a reporting API: impressions, clicks, spend and attributed conversions by day or hour, at campaign, ad set and ad level, with breakdowns such as placement, country and age range. They expect today's numbers within {{freshness}}. Numbers for a day keep changing for {{restate_days}}: conversions are attributed after the fact, and impressions and clicks judged invalid are removed and their charges reversed.
sections.problem: Design the pipeline from delivery and billing events to these reports. Cover the storage grain that lets every account see its own days and hours, daylight-saving days, the near-real-time path and the settled path, how restatements flow into reports and exports, how spend in the reports reconciles with what the advertiser is billed, how large accounts are served, and how an advertiser who downloaded yesterday's numbers can tell that they changed.
sections.constraints: Every account's "day" is midnight to midnight in its own time zone, including zones whose offset from UTC is not a whole number of hours. Spend is in the account's currency, in minor units, and the settled daily spend must equal what billing charges for that day. Breakdowns by age range or country follow minimum-count rules, so no report reveals a handful of people. Reports must be consistent: totals equal the sum of their rows within one response.
sections.assumptions: Volumes and timings are hypothetical. Attribution and invalid-activity detection are separate systems that publish their results as events; you do not design them. Assume an account's time zone does not change after creation in this exercise.
sections.criteria: UTC event time stored at a grain every offset divides (15 minutes), with local days computed per account at query or rollup time; correct DST handling with an explicit rule for repeated and missing hours; near-real-time and settled paths with a clear handover; restatements as new versions within the window, and a defined policy after it; spend in minor units reconciled with billing per day and currency; breakdown thresholds; consistent responses for large accounts; capacity reasoning at {{daily_impressions}} impressions a day.

clarifications.q: Which time zones must work?
clarifications.a: All of them, including offsets of 30 and 45 minutes from UTC, and zones with daylight-saving time.

clarifications.q: What does a report show for the hour that repeats when clocks go back?
clarifications.a: Decide and state it: for example two rows labelled with their UTC offset, or one merged row with a note. The daily total must be right either way.

clarifications.q: Is a conversion reported on the day of the conversion or the day of the ad impression or click?
clarifications.a: Both views exist; the default is the day of the impression or click. Your design should support both without a separate pipeline.

clarifications.q: Do reports need to match the invoice to the minor unit?
clarifications.a: Settled daily spend does. Today's near-real-time spend is labelled as an estimate.

clarifications.q: How large is the largest account?
clarifications.a: About 1% of all impressions, with hundreds of thousands of ads.

hints: A UTC hour does not map to one local day for every zone. Choose a stored time grain that every offset in use divides.
Keep a near-real-time aggregate for today and a settled aggregate rebuilt from the full event history for days still inside the restatement window; serve the settled one when it exists.
Version settled days. An export carries the version it was taken from, so a later restatement is visible rather than silent.
followups: Walk through how one impression at 23:50 UTC appears in the daily report of an account in UTC+05:30 and one in UTC−08:00, from event to report row.

An invalid-activity sweep removes 2% of an account's clicks from 5 days ago and reverses their charges. Which tables change, what does the advertiser see, and what happens to an export they downloaded last week?
The reporting API returns ad-level hourly rows with an age-range breakdown for an account with 300 000 ads. How do you make that response fast and consistent?
Finance reports that settled spend for one currency is 0.03% higher than billing every day. How do you find the cause?
Supporting a time zone change for an account becomes a product requirement. What breaks in your design, and what would you change?

rules.ask: An account is in UTC+05:45. Which UTC hours belong to its Tuesday, and how does an hourly UTC table answer that?
You store the local date per event. What happens when the same event must appear in reports for two views with different time zones, or when a zone's rules change?
An advertiser exported Monday's numbers on Wednesday and again on Friday, and they differ. How do they find out what changed and why?
Spend is billed in minor units. Where does rounding happen in your pipeline, and how do you keep the daily total equal to billing?
How many combinations of level, breakdown, grain and time zone does that produce for {{ad_accounts}} accounts, and which do you actually need to store?

incidents: On the night clocks go back in one region, advertisers in that region see 25 hours in Sunday's hourly report, and one reports that an hour of spend was charged twice.
An invalid-activity sweep arrives a day after the {{restate_days}} restatement window closed, for spend that was already invoiced.
A large advertiser's nightly API export of ad-level hourly rows with breakdowns starts timing out after it doubled its number of ads.

templates.title: Friendship-graph clusters for network experiments, rebuilt nightly
templates.subtopic: iterative Spark jobs, skew, stability across runs

sections.scenario: A social network tests changes to features where one person's experience depends on their friends' — a new way to share, for example. If friends land in different experiment groups, the groups influence each other and the measured effect is biased. A common remedy, described in public research on network experiments, is to randomise whole clusters of closely connected people rather than individuals. The experimentation team wants a cluster assignment for the {{users}} people in the friendship graph (about {{avg_friends}} friends each on average), with clusters of roughly {{cluster_size}}, rebuilt every night within {{batch_window}} from the daily snapshot of the friendship table.
sections.problem: Design the batch pipeline that produces user → cluster every night. Cover how the snapshot is read and prepared, the clustering algorithm and how it runs on a distributed engine, how you keep cluster sizes in range, how you handle very high-degree accounts and skew, iterations, checkpoints and failure recovery, how the assignment stays stable from night to night, what running experiments see when clusters change, new and deleted accounts, and the quality metrics you publish with each run.
sections.constraints: At most {{max_churn}} of people may change cluster from one night to the next. An experiment that has started must keep the assignment it started with. Deleted accounts must leave the assignment table within the platform's deletion period. The job shares the cluster with other nightly work and must finish within {{batch_window}}, including retries.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, sizes and limits are hypothetical. Friendships are undirected and stored once per pair in the snapshot. The connected components of a social graph are dominated by one giant component, so components alone are not useful clusters; you need a partitioning method.
sections.criteria: Explains why components fail and why balanced partitioning is needed; a symmetric edge table prepared once; capacity-constrained label propagation (or a defended alternative) as iterative joins and aggregations; skew handling for very high-degree accounts; checkpointing and deterministic, seeded, resumable iterations; warm starts and an explicit churn limit; frozen, versioned assignments for running experiments; new and deleted accounts handled; published quality metrics (share of edges inside clusters, size distribution, churn) gating each run; finishes within {{batch_window}}, with capacity reasoning.

clarifications.q: Why not use connected components?
clarifications.a: Nearly everyone is in one giant component. The clusters need to be small and mostly closed: most friendships inside a cluster.

clarifications.q: Must clusters be exactly the same size?
clarifications.a: No. Roughly {{cluster_size}}, within a factor of two, so randomisation balances.

clarifications.q: What quality measure matters most?
clarifications.a: The share of friendships whose two ends are in the same cluster. Higher is better, subject to size limits.

clarifications.q: Can the algorithm be randomised?
clarifications.a: Yes, with a recorded seed, so a run can be reproduced exactly.

clarifications.q: What happens to people who join after an experiment started?
clarifications.a: Your design decides, and must explain how it avoids biasing that experiment.

hints: Label propagation fits a distributed engine: each person repeatedly adopts the label most common among their friends, subject to a capacity per label. Each iteration is one join and one aggregation.
Start from last night's labels instead of from scratch: it converges faster and keeps churn low.
Experiments read a frozen, versioned assignment taken when they start; the nightly job only changes the latest version.
followups: An account with 5 million friend-like connections sits in the graph. What does it do to your joins and to the clustering, and what do you do with it?
A night's run dies in iteration 9 of 12. How do you resume, and how do you make sure the result equals an uninterrupted run?
How would you show the experimentation team that the clusters are good enough, and that they did not get worse after a change to the algorithm?
The friendship graph grows by 0.5% a day. Instead of a nightly rebuild, how could you update clusters incrementally, and what would that do to churn?
A person deletes their account. Which tables and versions hold their cluster assignment, and what happens to running experiments that included them?

rules.ask: What is the size of the largest component in a social graph, and what would randomising it achieve?
How much shuffle does one iteration produce with {{users}} people and {{avg_friends}} friends each, and where do the most-connected accounts land?
Without a capacity limit, what do labels do on a social graph after many iterations?
Two consecutive runs with different random seeds move how many people between clusters, against your {{max_churn}} limit?
Why does lineage grow with each iteration in Spark, and what does a checkpoint cost you per iteration at this size?

incidents: After a holiday, a burst of new friendships makes the nightly job need 3 more iterations to converge, and it overruns its nightly window of {{batch_window}}.
A change to the snapshot export writes each friendship once in each direction for one night, doubling every person's degree.
An experiment's analysts report that one test group has 40% more people than the other, although randomisation was by cluster.

templates.title: Encrypted group chats — membership versions and per-device delivery state
templates.subtopic: versioned membership, fan-out state, idempotent receipts, minimisation

sections.scenario: A messaging app supports end-to-end encrypted group chats of up to {{group_size}} members; each member can have up to {{max_devices}} devices (a phone plus linked devices). About {{daily_group_messages}} group messages are sent a day. The sending app encrypts each message for a specific set of recipient devices, so the servers never see content, but they do hold what routing needs: groups, members, each account's device list, an opaque message id per send, and acknowledgements from devices. Members join, leave, are removed by admins, and link or unlink devices at any time. A device that is offline keeps its messages queued on the server for up to {{queue_days}} days. The sender can open "message info" to see how many recipients have it delivered and, when receipts are on, read.
sections.problem: Design the data model and the low-level write paths for group membership and delivery state. Cover: how membership and device lists are versioned; how a send is checked against the current membership so that exactly the right devices receive it; ordering within a group; the per-device queue entry, its lifecycle and when it is deleted; how acknowledgements and read receipts update "message info" exactly once; what the server still holds about a message one hour, one day and {{queue_days}} days after it was sent; and what account deletion and group deletion remove.
sections.constraints: A member removed from the group (or a device unlinked) must not be sent any message accepted after the removal. A newly linked device does not receive messages sent before it was linked. Message info reads p99 under 100 ms. The server keeps no message content and no delivery record longer than it needs to deliver and to serve message info.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, limits and the queue duration are hypothetical. How keys are distributed and rotated is out of scope; the model only has to tell the sender which devices to encrypt for and reject a send aimed at the wrong set. Read receipts can be turned off, in which case read events never arrive.
sections.criteria: Versioned membership and device lists with an atomic check at acceptance; a per-group order; per-device queue entries deleted on acknowledgement or expiry; exactly-once message info from deduplicated receipts; read receipts treated as possibly absent; minimal retention stated per table; deletion handled across membership, devices, queues and aggregates; each incident contained with a guardrail that would have caught it.

clarifications.q: Two admins change membership at the same moment as a send arrives. Who wins?
clarifications.a: Membership changes are serialised per group; the send must be judged against one specific membership version.

clarifications.q: What happens to a send encrypted for an out-of-date device list?
clarifications.a: The server rejects it with the current version, and the sending app re-encrypts for the new set and retries.

clarifications.q: Are messages ordered?
clarifications.a: Within a group, every member must see accepted messages in the same order.

clarifications.q: How long is message info available?
clarifications.a: As long as any recipient device can still acknowledge: up to {{queue_days}} days. After that it is final.

clarifications.q: Does a removed member lose messages already on their device?
clarifications.a: That is device-side and out of scope; the server must only stop sending.

hints: Treat membership as an append-only log of changes with a version number per group, plus a materialised current view. A send carries the version it was encrypted for; accept it with a compare-and-check against the current version.
The accepted send gets a per-group sequence number in the same step, which gives one order for everyone.
Message info is a small per-message aggregate updated from receipts that are deduplicated by (message, device), not a scan of the queue.
followups: An admin removes a member while a send to {{group_size}} members is being accepted. Walk through both requests and show which devices receive the message.
One group of {{group_size}} members with {{max_devices}} devices each is very active. Where do the per-group version check and sequence number become a bottleneck, and what would you change?
A device stays offline past {{queue_days}} days. What does its queue entry become, what does the sender's message info show, and what is left on the server?
A member deletes their account. List every table that references them (membership log, device list, queue entries, message info) and what happens to each.
A receipt arrives twice, and another arrives for a device that was unlinked after the message was accepted. What do your message-info counters do with each?

rules.ask: Your members table is updated in place. How does a send prove it was encrypted for the membership that was current when it was accepted?
A device's acknowledgement is retried after a timeout. What stops your counter from counting it twice, and how many bytes per message does that cost?
Two members send in the same millisecond to the same group. Which order do the other members see, and is it the same on every device?
A month after a message was delivered, what does the server still know about it, and why does it need to?
How many queue entries does one send to a full group create, and when is each one deleted?

incidents: A client release sends with a stale membership version and the server's check is accidentally skipped for one region; for two hours a member removed from groups of up to {{group_size}} people keeps receiving new messages encrypted for their devices.
After a retry storm, message info shows "delivered to" more devices than a group of {{group_size}} members with {{max_devices}} devices each can have.
The queue clean-up job uses the wrong unit and deletes undelivered entries after {{queue_days}} hours instead of days; devices that were offline over a weekend never receive those messages.

templates.title: A social graph edge model for friends, follows and blocks
templates.subtopic: graph edges, symmetric versus directed, edge history

sections.scenario: A social network has {{accounts}} accounts. Two kinds of connection coexist: a friendship is mutual and starts with a request that the other person accepts; a follow is one-way and needs no approval. An account can also block another, which hides each from the other. The average account has {{avg_friends}} friends, and the most-followed public accounts have up to {{top_followers}} followers. About {{edge_changes}} connections are created, removed or changed a day. Some accounts are private: following them needs the owner's approval, like a friend request. Product surfaces need friend lists, mutual-friend counts and follower counts; analysts need the graph as it was on any past date.
sections.problem: Design the edge model. Cover: how a friendship is stored (one row or two directed rows) and how both directions stay consistent; how friend requests, follows, follow requests to private accounts and blocks are represented and what a block does to existing friendships and follows; the access patterns and the keys that serve them ("is A friends with B", "A's friends, newest first", "mutual friends of A and B", "follower count of a public account"); how counts are maintained for accounts with {{top_followers}} followers; how edge history is kept so an analyst can ask "was A friends with B on 1 March"; and what account deletion does to every table.
sections.constraints: "Is A friends with B" and "list A's friends" are online reads with p99 under 20 ms. A block takes effect for both people before the next page load. Edge history must answer as-of questions for at least two years. Friendship is symmetric: no read path may ever see A→B without B→A.
sections.assumptions: Account counts, degrees and change rates are hypothetical. Online storage is a sharded key-value or relational store of your choice; the analytical copy lives in a columnar warehouse. Friend suggestions are out of scope.
sections.criteria: Symmetric edges stored and served consistently, with an explicit repair path for partial writes; follows, requests and blocks modelled distinctly with block semantics applied to both directions; keys designed from the stated access patterns; counters for high-degree accounts with reconciliation; separate current and interval history tables with non-overlapping intervals; deletion propagated through serving, counters and history; each incident contained and guarded.

clarifications.q: Can a pending friend request exist alongside a follow?
clarifications.a: Yes. Following someone and asking to be their friend are independent.

clarifications.q: What happens to a friendship when one side blocks the other?
clarifications.a: In this scenario the friendship ends and any follows in either direction are removed; unblocking does not restore them.

clarifications.q: Is there a friend limit?
clarifications.a: Assume a cap of 5,000 friends per account; follows are uncapped.

clarifications.q: Must the follower count be exact?
clarifications.a: Exact for the account itself within a minute; others may see a rounded figure such as "80M".

clarifications.q: Do deleted accounts' edges stay in history?
clarifications.a: Not in a form that identifies the deleted person. Say what you keep, if anything.

hints: Store the friendship as two directed rows keyed by the owner, so each person's friend list is one partition. Write both in one transaction when they share a shard; otherwise use an ordered, idempotent two-step write with a repair job.
Keep the current-edge table and the edge-history table separate: current for serving, history (one row per edge interval, with valid_from and valid_to) for as-of questions.
A follower count for a heavily followed account is a counter, not a COUNT(*). Decide how the counter is sharded and how it is reconciled with the edge rows.
followups: Your friendship write touches two shards and the second write fails. What do readers see in the meantime, and what repairs it?
"Mutual friends of A and B" with {{avg_friends}} friends each: walk through the read. What changes when one side has 5,000 friends?

A private account with 3,000 pending follow requests switches to public. What happens to the pending requests, to the follower count and to the history table, given {{edge_changes}} edge changes a day already flow through the pipeline?
A public account gains followers at 50,000 a minute after going viral. What happens to your follower counter and to the shard holding that account's follower list?
An analyst asks for the number of friendships that existed on 1 March, by country. Write the query shape against your history table and say what deletion did to the answer.

rules.ask: You store each friendship once, ordered by id. How does "list A's friends, newest first" read when A is sometimes the smaller id and sometimes the larger?
The second direction's write fails after the first commits. What does A see, what does B see, and what guarantees they converge?
That account has {{top_followers}} followers. What does a COUNT on every profile view cost, and what do you keep instead?
Which of the listed access patterns needs a graph traversal deeper than two hops? What would you lose by moving the online reads off a sharded key-value layout?
A deleted account's edges are flagged, not removed. Which reads must filter the flag, and how do you prove none forgets?

incidents: A deploy of the friendship service wrote only the first direction for 0.3% of new friendships for two hours; mutual-friend counts now differ depending on which person you ask, and the analytics copy shows friendships that the app does not.

A public account with {{top_followers}} followers is deleted; the deletion job fans out to every follower's edge rows, saturates the shard and delays blocks for other accounts on that shard by 40 minutes.

A unblock-then-refriend sequence on the same second was applied out of order by the history pipeline, leaving two overlapping valid intervals for one pair; the as-of friendship count for that day is now double-counting.

templates.title: Conversion lift studies — eligibility, assignment and opportunity logging
templates.subtopic: randomised experiments, sticky assignment, versioned study config

sections.scenario: An ads platform lets advertisers measure the causal effect of their ads with conversion lift studies. People who could be reached by the study's ads are randomly split: a holdout group ({{holdout_share}}) is never shown those ads, and the rest is eligible to see them. Conversions (purchases, sign-ups) are compared between the groups. A study can have {{cells}} cells (for example two creative strategies), each with its own holdout. Up to {{concurrent_studies}} studies run at once; one person can be in studies from different advertisers, but in this scenario two studies from the same advertiser must never share people. A study's population can reach {{population}} people.
sections.problem: Design the data model for lift studies. Cover: the study definition and which changes are allowed after it starts (and how they are versioned); when a person enters the study (at study start, or at their first ad opportunity) and what that choice does to the estimate; how assignment is made deterministic and sticky across devices and surfaces; what is logged at each ad opportunity for both test and holdout people; how conversions are joined to assignment; the analysis tables (conversions per group and cell, incremental conversions, an interval); how contamination (a holdout person shown a study ad) is detected and reported; and what advertisers see.
sections.constraints: A person's assignment never changes during a study. Results must be reproducible from the stored data. Advertisers see only aggregates, never who converted, and no cell covering fewer than a minimum number of people. Exclusivity between one advertiser's overlapping studies is guaranteed at assignment time.
sections.assumptions: Population sizes, shares, cell counts and the number of concurrent studies are hypothetical. People are identified by the platform's own logged-in identity across devices. Conversions arrive already deduplicated and matched to people; that pipeline is out of scope.
sections.criteria: Versioned study config with changes classed as allowed or forbidden after start; an explicit population definition and its bias/noise trade-off; deterministic, sticky, exclusive assignment; opportunity logging for both groups; intention-to-treat analysis with an interval and a stopping rule; contamination measured and reported; minimisation and small-cell suppression in advertiser output; each incident handled with containment and an honest statement about the result's validity.

clarifications.q: Is the population everyone the campaign targets, or only people who reached an ad opportunity?
clarifications.a: Your choice. Say what each does to the estimate's noise and to the data you must log.

clarifications.q: Can the advertiser change targeting or budget during the study?
clarifications.a: Budget and creative yes, as new config versions. Changing the holdout share or the cells after start is not allowed.

clarifications.q: Does a holdout person see other ads?
clarifications.a: Yes. Only the study's ads are withheld; the auction fills the slot with another ad.

clarifications.q: How long after the study ends do conversions count?
clarifications.a: For a fixed post-period defined in the study config, then the result is final.

clarifications.q: What if a person deletes their account during the study?
clarifications.a: Their data leaves the study; say what that does to a published result.

hints: Assignment can be computed instead of stored: hash(study salt, person) into buckets, with the cut-points in the study version. Record the first assignment event anyway; analysis should not depend on recomputing a hash with today's config.

Log the same opportunity record for both groups at the moment the holdout check runs, with the group, the would-be ad, and whether it was served. Then the two groups can be compared on the same footing.
Analyse by assigned group (intention to treat), not by whether the person saw an ad.
followups: Compare "everyone targeted at study start" with "people who reached an ad opportunity" as the study population. Which has less noise, which needs more logging, and which can be biased by the ads themselves?
With {{concurrent_studies}} concurrent studies, how do you guarantee that two studies from the same advertiser never assign the same person, without a global lock?

Compute incremental conversions and a confidence interval for one cell with a {{holdout_share}} holdout. What changes with {{cells}} cells compared at once, and with an advertiser checking the result every day?
The advertiser doubles the budget halfway through. What is versioned, what is reported, and is the study still valid?
A person in the holdout deletes their account two days before the study ends. What happens to stored opportunities, conversions and the already-published interim result?

rules.ask: You compare people who saw the ad with people who did not. Who chose who saw it, and why is that not the lift?
The assignment service restarts and recomputes. Does the same person land in the same group, on every device and surface?
A study has {{population}} people. Do you store every assignment, compute it on demand, or both? What does analysis read?
The advertiser checks the result every morning and stops when it looks significant. What does that do to the error rate, and what do you show instead?
Which tables contain person identifiers, who can query them, and what does the advertiser's report contain instead?

incidents: A configuration change rotated a study's salt mid-flight; about {{holdout_share}} of people were re-randomised, and some who had been in the holdout started receiving the study's ads.
A newly launched ad placement skipped the holdout check, so holdout people saw study ads there for four days; the measured lift falls and the advertiser asks whether to trust any of it.
One of {{cells}} cells in a small study reports conversions for a group of nine people, and an advertiser asks why one identifiable customer appears in the converted count.

templates.title: Stories that expire — audiences, viewer lists and highlights
templates.subtopic: time-bounded visibility, audience lists, viewer receipts, retention

sections.scenario: A photo and video app lets people post stories: photos or short videos that others can see for 24 hours. A story is shared with all followers or with a "close friends" list of up to {{close_friends_cap}} people that the author maintains; the author can also hide stories from chosen people, and a block hides everything. The author can see who viewed each story for {{viewer_list_hours}} hours after posting. After 24 hours the story disappears for everyone else but stays in the author's private archive, and the author can add it to a highlight on their profile, where it stays visible until removed. About {{daily_stories}} stories are posted a day; the largest accounts get up to {{top_viewers}} viewers per story.
sections.problem: Design the data model and the read and write paths. Cover: the story item and the media it points to; how the audience is decided (at posting time, at viewing time, or both) and what happens when a close-friends list, a hide list or a block changes while a story is live; how expiry is enforced to the second; the viewer receipt (one per viewer per story, ordering, deduplication) and how its retention of {{viewer_list_hours}} hours is enforced; how archive and highlights reuse the media without reusing the story's visibility rules; what deleting a story, a highlight or a whole account removes, including the author's own appearances in other people's viewer lists; and what aggregate story metrics may be kept after viewer identities are gone.
sections.constraints: Nobody but the author sees a story after 24 hours from posting, whether or not any clean-up job has run. A person removed from the audience (removed from close friends, added to the hide list, or blocked) must not be able to open the story on their next request. Only the author can see the viewer list. Viewer identities are not kept beyond {{viewer_list_hours}} hours; counts may be.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, list sizes and retention are hypothetical. Media storage and delivery are out of scope beyond the reference to a media object. Replies to a story are delivered as messages and are out of scope.
sections.criteria: Expiry and audience enforced on read with server time; audience removals and blocks effective immediately, with caches and media links handled; one receipt per (story, viewer) with a sensible key and hot-story handling; viewer identities removed on schedule with counts kept; media referenced by story, archive and highlight with separate visibility; deletion complete in both directions; each incident contained, quantified and guarded.

clarifications.q: A person is added to close friends while a close-friends story is live. Can they see it?
clarifications.a: Your choice; say which you chose and why. Removal, though, must take effect immediately.

clarifications.q: Does the author's own view count?
clarifications.a: No, and the author never appears in their own viewer list.

clarifications.q: A viewer opens the same story six times. How many receipts?
clarifications.a: One per viewer per story in the list; you may keep a count or the last view time.

clarifications.q: Who can see a highlight?
clarifications.a: In this scenario, the author's current followers, subject to blocks; highlights have no viewer list.

clarifications.q: Which clock decides expiry?
clarifications.a: The server's time of posting plus 24 hours. Device clocks are not trusted.

hints: Make expiry and audience part of the read predicate (posted_at + 24h > now() and the audience check). Deletion jobs only reclaim storage; they are never what hides a story.
Store the audience as a reference to the list plus the list's version at posting time, and re-check removals at read time against the current list, hide list and blocks.
Media is one object; the story, the archive entry and each highlight item are separate rows that reference it, each with its own visibility.
followups: The author removes someone from close friends while a close-friends story is live and that person has the story tray cached in their app. Walk through what they can and cannot open.
A story on an account with {{top_viewers}} viewers: how do you write receipts without a hot partition, and how does the author page through the viewer list?
The author adds an expired story to a highlight. Which fields are copied, which are referenced, and who can now see it?
An account is deleted. List what goes: its stories, archive, highlights, viewer lists of its own stories, and its receipts in other people's viewer lists.
Product wants daily reach and completion for stories by country. What do you aggregate, when, and at what threshold, so the aggregate survives the {{viewer_list_hours}}-hour limit on identities?

rules.ask: The clean-up job is three hours behind. What does a follower see 25 hours after posting, and what in your design guarantees it?
You snapshot the audience at posting. The author blocks someone an hour later. What stops that person from opening the story?
The same person views a story six times, from two devices, during a retry. How many rows, and what key makes that true?
The story is also in the archive and in a highlight. What exactly does "delete this story" remove, and what does "delete this highlight" remove?
Media URLs are cached at the edge. How does a removed viewer get blocked from media they already have a link to?

incidents: The story tray in the app is cached for 10 minutes; a person removed from close friends kept opening a close-friends story during that window, and the author reports it as a privacy failure.
The job that removes viewer identities after {{viewer_list_hours}} hours silently failed for nine days; identities of viewers of about {{daily_stories}} stories a day are still stored.
Two regions disagree by several minutes on time, and some stories stay openable for a few minutes past 24 hours in one of them.

templates.title: Creator audience insights with a privacy threshold and deletion
templates.subtopic: k-anonymity thresholds, complementary suppression, deletion, as-of dimensions

sections.scenario: A photo and video app gives creators weekly audience insights for their short videos (reels): how many distinct people watched, broken down by age band. Small groups must not be identifiable, so the insights apply a privacy threshold of k = {{k}} people. Account deletion is first marked in accounts.deleted_at and purged from the raw view log by a later job; the insights must already treat a deleted account as gone. Ages are kept only as bands in age_band_history, one row per band an account has been in, from its valid_from. {{band_note}}
sections.problem:
Write one PostgreSQL query for the week from {{start}} (inclusive) to {{end}} (exclusive) that returns creator_id, age_band, viewers, ordered by creator_id, age_band. The rules:

  • An eligible view is a row of reel_views with viewed_at in the week, on a reel (reels.creator_id) whose creator is not deleted, by a viewer who is not deleted (deleted_at IS NULL) and is not the creator. Any recorded view counts, whatever its watch_ms.
  • A viewer's band is the age_band of their age_band_history row in effect at {{end}}: the row with the latest valid_from at or before {{end}}.
  • For each creator, one row per age band that has at least one eligible viewer, with viewers = the number of distinct eligible viewers in that band; and one row with age_band = 'all' and the number of distinct eligible viewers overall.
  • A band row with fewer than {{k}} viewers is published with viewers NULL. If exactly one band row of a creator is NULL by that rule, also set viewers NULL on the creator's band row with the smallest count among the rest (ties: the first age_band in sort order), so that 'all' minus the published bands cannot reveal it.
  • A creator whose 'all' count is below {{k}} gets no rows at all.
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). The extract has {{accounts}} accounts and {{views}} views; production has billions of views a week, so say how your query would scale. age_band values sort as text ('13-17' … '55+', then 'all').
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical schema, accounts, threshold and data. All timestamps are UTC. Every account has a band row in effect at the end of the week. Every deletion recorded in accounts happened before this report runs.
sections.criteria: Eligibility applied once (week boundaries, self-views, deleted viewers and creators); distinct viewers, not views; the band in effect at the end time with an inclusive valid_from; threshold inclusive at k; complementary suppression with the stated tie-break; creators below k omitted; deterministic order; can explain differencing attacks, deletion guarantees and approximate counts.

clarifications.q: A viewer watched three of a creator's reels. How many viewers is that?
clarifications.a: One. Viewers are distinct people per creator.

clarifications.q: A deleted account viewed reels before it was deleted. Do those views count?
clarifications.a: No. A deleted account leaves every derived number, including for views from before its deletion.

clarifications.q: Is a band with exactly k viewers published?
clarifications.a: Yes. Only counts below k are suppressed.

clarifications.q: A creator has two bands below k. Do I suppress a third?
clarifications.a: No. Complementary suppression applies only when exactly one band is below k.

clarifications.q: A view at exactly the end time?
clarifications.a: It belongs to the next week. A view at exactly the start time belongs to this week.

hints: Build the distinct (creator, viewer) pairs first, applying every eligibility rule once; everything else is aggregation over that set.
DISTINCT ON (account_id) … ORDER BY account_id, valid_from DESC with valid_from <= end picks the band in effect.
For the complementary cell, rank each creator's published cells by (viewers, age_band) with ROW_NUMBER() and count the suppressed cells per creator with a window or a join.
followups: The report is also produced daily over a sliding 7-day window. Show how two consecutive daily reports, each correctly suppressed, can still reveal one viewer by differencing, and what you would change.
Deletion is marked in accounts and purged later. What guarantees that no derived table or cached report keeps a deleted account's contribution after the purge deadline?
At billions of views a week, which pre-aggregate would you keep (and at what grain) so this query does not scan raw views, without breaking distinct counting?
Product asks for the threshold on approximate distinct counts (HyperLogLog sketches). What goes wrong with a threshold applied to an estimate, and how do you make suppression safe?

rules.ask: One person watched a creator's reels five times. How many does your count report, and what should a privacy threshold be counting?
You keep views from before the deletion. What does the person who deleted their account expect to happen to those views?

Is your HAVING applied to band cells or to the creator's total? A small band is published as NULL, a small creator disappears: which does your query do to each, and what could a creator learn by subtracting?
A viewer turned 18 the day after the week ended. Which band does your query put them in, and which should it?

incidents: The purge job for the raw view log falls three weeks behind; a privacy review asks whether any weekly insight published in that period counted deleted accounts, and how you would prove it from the tables alone.
A creator compares the weekly insights with a daily insight that has a different threshold and recovers the age band of a single viewer in a band that the weekly report suppressed with k = {{k}}.

templates.title: Experiment scorecards for feed ranking changes, with network effects
templates.subtopic: metric pipelines, variance, interference on a social graph

sections.scenario: Teams that work on a social app's feed ranking run about {{experiments}} randomised experiments at once over {{daily_users}} daily users. A person is in many experiments at the same time, in different layers; within a layer, experiments do not overlap. Each experiment has a scorecard of {{metrics}} metrics (time spent, sessions, posts viewed, likes, comments, posts created, hides, reports, ratios such as likes per post viewed) for each arm, with confidence intervals, daily and cumulative since launch, ready within {{results_by}} after each UTC day ends. Because people interact, a change shown to the treatment arm can change what their friends in the control arm see and do: a ranking change that produces more comments also produces more replies from friends.
sections.problem: Design the pipeline that produces these scorecards. Cover how assignment and exposure are recorded, how raw events become metrics without scanning raw logs once per experiment, how ratio metrics and confidence intervals are computed, cumulative results, variance reduction, data-quality gates, experiments randomised by clusters of connected people rather than by person, recomputation when a metric definition is fixed, and the cost at this scale.
sections.constraints: Every scorecard number must be reproducible from a versioned metric definition and the data. The raw event logs are too large to scan once per experiment. A scorecard must not be shown as decision-ready if the experiment fails a data-quality check. Teams look at results every day.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, counts and deadlines are hypothetical. Assignment is a deterministic hash of the person and a layer salt; the experiment's code path logs an exposure event when the person actually reaches it.
