sections.criteria: One aggregation pass into a per-person-day table with versioned metric definitions; experiments computed from exposures and sufficient statistics; correct variance for ratio metrics and for cluster randomisation; incremental cumulative results; variance reduction with pre-period data; automatic quality gates (sample ratio, exposure completeness) that block scorecards; a policy for daily peeking; interference detection; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Who is in an experiment's analysis?
clarifications.a: People who were exposed (reached the changed code path) at least once, from their first exposure onward, in the arm they were assigned.

clarifications.q: Are ratio metrics computed per post viewed?
clarifications.a: They are defined as total numerator over total denominator within an arm, but the person is the randomisation unit.

clarifications.q: How are cluster experiments randomised?
clarifications.a: Groups of densely connected people are assigned together; you decide how the analysis treats them.

clarifications.q: How often do metric definitions change?
clarifications.a: Weekly. A fix to a definition sometimes needs past results recomputed.

clarifications.q: Can a scorecard use data from before the experiment?
clarifications.a: Yes, pre-experiment behaviour of the same people is available.

hints: Aggregate raw events once into a per-person-per-day metric table; every experiment then joins its exposures to that table. Cost then scales with people and metrics, not with experiments times raw events.
A confidence interval needs only a few sums per arm (count, sum, sum of squares, and cross-products for ratios). Decide where per-person values are still needed.
When the unit you randomise is not the unit you count, the variance must follow the randomisation unit.
followups: How do you compute cumulative results since launch for {{experiments}} experiments without recomputing every person's full history each day?
Likes per post viewed is a ratio of two per-person sums. How do you compute its confidence interval, and why is treating every post view as independent wrong?
The split is configured 50/50, and an experiment with 100 million people shows 50.6% versus 49.4%. What does that mean, and what does the platform do?
How do you detect that control people are affected by treatment through their friends, and what does cluster randomisation cost in statistical power?
Teams check scorecards every day and ship when something looks significant. How does the platform keep false positives honest?

rules.ask: Likes per post viewed is a ratio of per-person sums. Which variance goes into your test, and what happens if you use post views as the units?
How many rows is that per day at {{daily_users}} users and {{metrics}} metrics, and how do you join it to {{experiments}} experiments without one scan per experiment?
New people joined last week and have no pre-period data. What does your adjustment do for them?
If you randomise a few hundred thousand clusters instead of hundreds of millions of people, what happens to the width of your intervals?
Exposure is logged by the app. If one app version drops exposure events in one arm only, what does every metric in that experiment show?

incidents: An app release stops logging exposures for the treatment arm on one platform. A large experiment shows 51.2% versus 48.8% and a +3% time-spent gain, and leadership has already seen the daily scorecard.

The job that builds the per-person-per-day table is held up by a skewed partition: a few thousand automated accounts with millions of events each. Scorecards for all {{experiments}} experiments miss the {{results_by}} target.
A comment-ranking experiment reports +4% comments in treatment, but control people's comments also rose compared with their own pre-period. Product asks whether the effect is real.

templates.title: Spam signals for encrypted messaging, from metadata and reports
templates.subtopic: sliding windows, labels and feedback, privacy without content

sections.scenario: A messaging app carries about {{daily_messages}} messages a day, all end-to-end encrypted, so servers never see content. Spammers register accounts (about {{new_accounts}} new accounts of all kinds are registered per day) and send unsolicited bulk messages. What servers can see is metadata: account age and registration details, how many messages an account sends and to how many distinct recipients, whether a recipient has exchanged messages with the sender before, group creations and invitations, and how often recipients block or report the sender. When someone reports an account, the report can include recent messages that the reporting person chooses to share. The integrity team wants to act on a bulk-messaging account within {{act_within}} of the behaviour starting, while legitimate heavy users (community organisers, small businesses, new users inviting friends) are left alone. Human reviewers can look at about {{reviews}} cases a day.
sections.problem: Design the system: the metadata events and features, how per-account features over sliding windows are computed in real time, scoring, the ladder of enforcement actions, the review and appeal loop, where labels come from and how they bias the model, how you measure precision and the prevalence of spam, how coordinated campaigns across many accounts are found, and how the data is minimised and retained.
sections.constraints: No message content, except what a reporting person shares in a report. Records that link a sender to a recipient are kept at most 72 hours. Every enforcement action stores the signals and the rule or model version that caused it, so an appeal can be decided. Automatic permanent bans must have a measured false-positive rate below an agreed target.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, rates and capacities are hypothetical. Registered business senders that use a separate business interface are out of scope.
sections.criteria: Content-free features from metadata with explicit retention for sender-recipient links; real-time sliding-window features keyed by sender; an action ladder matched to confidence and reversibility; labels, appeals and a random review sample with stated bias; precision and prevalence measured; cluster-level detection for coordinated campaigns; explainable, auditable actions; staleness monitoring; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Does the server know whether two people have talked before?
clarifications.a: Delivery metadata can tell whether a conversation already exists; how long you keep that knowledge is part of your design.

clarifications.q: What actions are available?
clarifications.a: Slowing an account's sending, requiring re-verification, temporary restrictions, and bans. Each has a different cost if wrong.

clarifications.q: Where do labels come from?
clarifications.a: Reviewer decisions, appeal outcomes and reports. Reports alone are noisy and can be abused.

clarifications.q: Can reviewers see the account's messages?
clarifications.a: Only messages shared in a report.

hints: Key the stream by sender and keep features for several window lengths; distinct recipients per window can be counted with a small sketch.
Spend certainty where it is cheap: soft actions at moderate scores, irreversible ones only at high confidence or after review.
Labels exist mostly for accounts you already acted on. Keep a random sample of reviews to measure what you miss.
followups: Size the feature state: windows of 1 minute, 10 minutes, 1 hour and 1 day for every sending account, with distinct-recipient counts. How large is it, and how is it partitioned?
A campaign spreads sending across thousands of new accounts, each under every per-account threshold. What finds it?
How do you estimate precision, recall and the overall prevalence of spam when nearly all labels come from accounts you already restricted?
A community organiser messages 400 people who have not talked to them before, the evening before an event. Why does your system not ban them?
An appeal asks why the account was restricted. What can you show without teaching spammers your thresholds or revealing anything about other people?

rules.ask: Your labels come from accounts you already banned. What does the model learn, and how do you find spam it has never seen?
Thousands of legitimate people can share one public address behind a carrier. What does acting on that signal alone do?
With {{reviews}} reviews a day, which actions happen without a human, and what false-positive rate do you accept for each?
A group can mass-report someone it dislikes. How do you weight reports so that cannot be used as a weapon?
That store records who talks to whom. Why is that sensitive without content, and how long may it live?

incidents: A coordinated campaign spreads its sending across 40,000 new accounts, each staying under every per-account threshold. Reports rise sharply, but no account reaches the ban score.
A threshold change restricts a wave of legitimate accounts in one country on a holiday when people traditionally message many contacts in an hour. Appeals exceed {{reviews}} a day within hours.
The feature pipeline in one region falls 25 minutes behind. Scores are computed on stale features, and action within {{act_within}} silently stops there.

templates.title: Ad conversion attribution with click and view windows
templates.subtopic: windowed attribution joins, deduplication, restatement

sections.scenario: An ads platform serves about {{daily_impressions}} ad impressions a day across its apps. Advertisers send conversion events (purchase, lead, sign-up) from their websites through a browser tag and from their own servers through a server-to-server API, with customer identifiers hashed before sending. About {{dup_share}} of conversions arrive through both routes; advertisers are asked to send the same event id on both so the two can be deduplicated. Around {{daily_conversions}} conversions arrive per day, and about {{late_share}} arrive more than a day after they happened. For this exercise the attribution rule is: credit the last click on the advertiser's ad within {{click_window}} before the conversion; if there is none, the last view within 1 day. Advertisers see conversions and conversion value per campaign, ad set and ad, by day, and the ad delivery system wants conversions quickly to optimise bids.
sections.problem: Design the attribution system: conversion intake and deduplication, matching conversions to people, storing clicks and views for the window, the attribution join, which day a conversion is reported on, restating reports when late data arrives, the reporting store, a fast feed for delivery optimisation, and privacy in reporting.
sections.constraints: A conversion is counted once even if received twice, and credited to at most one ad. Attribution is deterministic: rerunning it on the same inputs gives the same answer. Advertisers see only aggregates, never which person converted, and small cells are suppressed. Reported days may change for 7 days after they end and are final afterwards.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, windows and shares are hypothetical, and the attribution rule above is a simplified rule for this exercise. Identity matching returns a person id or nothing; some conversions never match.
sections.criteria: Deterministic, idempotent attribution keyed on a stable conversion identity; bounded dedup with precedence and a policy for missing event ids; an interaction index with a TTL equal to the longest window; credit assigned once per conversion across the advertiser's ads; explicit reporting date and restatement period; separate provisional and final signals for delivery; aggregate-only reporting with small-cell suppression; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Is a conversion reported on the day of the conversion or the day of the ad interaction?
clarifications.a: Both conventions exist. Choose one, say why, and say what it means for restatement.

clarifications.q: Can a conversion be credited to another advertiser's ad?
clarifications.a: No. Only the reporting advertiser's ads are candidates.

clarifications.q: What if the browser event and the server event disagree on value?
clarifications.a: Decide a precedence and make it deterministic.

clarifications.q: How fast does delivery optimisation need conversions?
clarifications.a: Within 30 minutes would help; it can accept a provisional signal that is corrected later.

clarifications.q: Can an advertiser change the attribution setting?
clarifications.a: Yes, per ad set, at any time. Decide what happens to history.

hints: Index ad interactions by (advertiser, person) and keep them only as long as the longest window; the conversion looks backwards into that index.
Deduplicate on a key the advertiser controls (data source, event name, event id) within a bounded window, and decide what an advertiser who never sends an event id gets.
Make attribution a pure function of the conversion and the interactions known at a cutoff, so a rerun after late data replaces earlier output rather than adding to it.
followups: The browser event arrives at 10:00 and the server event for the same purchase at 13:00 with a different value. Which wins, and how long is your dedup window?
A click that happened six days before a conversion arrives late, after you already credited a view from yesterday. What changes, in which report, and what does the advertiser see?
An advertiser has ten campaigns that all reached the same person. How do you make sure the conversion is credited once across them, and what does each campaign's conversions column show?
An advertiser changes an ad set's click window from {{click_window}} to a different length mid-flight. Do you recompute history? What does that cost?
Delivery wants conversions within 30 minutes, but dedup and late matching need hours. How do you give delivery a signal now and correct it later without the bidder overreacting?

rules.ask: The click arrives after you have already credited a view. Does a rerun give the same answer as the live path, and which one is the truth?
An advertiser sends no event ids. What do you deduplicate on, and how many false merges does that create for a shop whose customers often buy the same item twice?
How much click and view state must you hold for a {{click_window}} click window at {{daily_impressions}} impressions a day, and how is it partitioned?
An advertiser asks for the list of people who converted. What do you return, and why?
Under your choice, which past days change when a conversion arrives five days late, and how far back can restatement reach?

incidents: After a deploy, a large advertiser's server integration sends every purchase twice with different event ids. Their reported conversions double overnight and automated bidding starts spending more on their campaigns.

A regional outage delays conversion intake for 30 hours. When the backlog drains, yesterday's report, which many advertisers had already exported, rises by 12%; this week far more than the usual {{late_share}} of conversions arrive late.
The matching service changes how it normalises hashed email addresses. The match rate jumps by 8% in one day, and attributed conversions jump with it for every advertiser.

templates.title: Deletion propagation across the warehouse, streams and training data
templates.subtopic: deletion at scale in columnar storage, lineage, verification

sections.scenario: People can delete posts, comments and whole accounts across the company's apps. About {{account_deletions}} accounts and {{content_deletions}} content items are deleted per day. The company commits that deleted data is removed from its systems within {{window_days}} days. Product databases handle their own deletion; your scope is everything downstream: event streams, a lakehouse with {{tables}} tables (raw events, derived tables, aggregates), feature tables and training datasets for ranking models, analysts' scratch tables and extracts, and backups.
sections.problem: Design the deletion propagation system for this estate: how you know where a person's or a post's data lives, the deletion request log, how deletes are executed efficiently in large columnar tables, what happens to derived tables and aggregates, streams and their retention, training datasets and models already trained, backups and restores, verification with evidence per request, and how new tables are covered from the day they are created.
sections.constraints: Every request completes within {{window_days}} days, including physical removal from storage files. Completion must be verifiable per request. Rewriting every large table every day is not affordable. For this exercise, an aggregate may be kept after a deletion if each of its cells covers at least 100 people.
sections.assumptions: All volumes and counts are hypothetical. Tables use account ids, but some use device ids, hashed ids or ids nested inside semi-structured columns. Backups follow their own documented retention cycle.
sections.criteria: Classification at creation plus scanning; a durable request log and batched deletes per table; layout chosen to bound rewrite cost; physical removal tracked to completion; aggregates handled by an explicit rule; streams retained within the window; datasets purged before training and a stated model policy; restores that replay deletions; per-request evidence; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Do aggregates have to be recomputed?
clarifications.a: Only cells that could identify someone under the 100-person rule; larger cells may stay.

clarifications.q: What about models trained on deleted data?
clarifications.a: For this exercise, training datasets must be purged before the next training run, and models are retrained on their regular cadence, which is shorter than {{window_days}} days. Say if you think that is not enough.

clarifications.q: Who owns each table?
clarifications.a: Thousands of teams. Many tables have no clear owner today.

clarifications.q: How do analysts create tables?
clarifications.a: Mostly through scheduled pipelines, but also by ad hoc queries that create tables from other tables.

hints: A deletion run is a join: the batch of requests against each table's identifier columns. Batch requests per table so each file is rewritten at most once per cycle.
Whether a delete touches ten files or ten thousand depends on how the table is laid out; date-only partitioning spreads one person across every partition.
You cannot delete what you cannot find. Classification has to happen when a table is created, with scanning to catch what slipped through.
followups: A 200 TB event table is partitioned by date only. One day's batch of deletions touches every partition. What do you change in the layout or the method, and what does each option cost?
Some identifiers sit inside semi-structured columns, and some tables hold device ids linked to accounts. How do you find and delete those rows?
Show the evidence you would produce that request R is complete everywhere, including physical removal.
A ranking model was trained last week on data from accounts deleted since. What is required, and what would you push back on?
A backup from 20 days ago is restored after an accident. How do you guarantee that deleted data does not come back?

rules.ask: Each delete rewrites every file that holds a matching row. How many files does one day's batch touch in a date-partitioned table, and what does that cost?
The rows are hidden from readers but still inside the files until compaction. When are they physically gone, and does that meet {{window_days}} days?
An analyst created a table from a registered one with an ad hoc query. Does your lineage see it, and who owns its deletion?
One key per person across {{tables}} tables: what does every query pay, and what about derived tables that combine many people?
One cell of an aggregate counts 3 people, one of whom deleted their account. Does that cell stay?

incidents: The compaction job that physically removes deleted rows has been failing quietly in one storage region for three weeks. Rows are hidden from queries but still in the files, and the {{window_days}}-day deadline arrives for the oldest requests in nine days.
A team created 40 tables from copies of registered tables through ad hoc queries; none was registered for deletion. It is discovered two months later.
A backup restore after an accidental table drop brings back rows for 60,000 accounts deleted since the backup was taken.

templates.title: Social context on feed posts: which of your friends reacted
templates.subtopic: fan-out on write versus read-time intersection, hot posts, freshness

sections.scenario: Under each post in a social app's feed, the app shows social context: "Priya, Sam and 14 other friends reacted". It names up to two friends of the viewer who reacted to or commented on the post, chosen by how close they are to the viewer, and counts the rest. People make about {{daily_reactions}} reactions and comments a day; the average person has {{avg_friends}} friends and nobody has more than 5,000; the most popular posts collect {{top_reactions}} reactions. The feed renders about {{renders}} posts per second at peak, and social context must be ready within {{latency}} at p99 per post, inside the feed's own budget.
sections.problem: Design how social context is computed and served: the data each side holds (a person's friends, a post's reactors), whether you push each reaction to the reactor's friends when it happens or intersect at read time (or a hybrid), how names are chosen, how counts stay correct, how removals (un-reacting, unfriending, blocking, deleted accounts) take effect, caching, and cost.
sections.constraints: A removed reaction, an unfriending or a block is reflected within one minute. The count shown must never be higher than the true number. Never name a person the viewer has blocked or who has blocked the viewer, and never name a reaction the viewer is not allowed to see. p99 within {{latency}} per post.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, limits and budgets are hypothetical. Friend lists live in a sharded online store; reactions are written to a log and to a store keyed by post. A closeness score between two friends is available from another system.
sections.criteria: Quantifies write amplification and read cost before choosing; picks the cheaper side per post (fetch a small reactor list and intersect with the viewer's friend set; for a large one, send the friend list to where the reactor set lives), or a fan-out design whose write cost is justified; screening with confirmation for very large sets; never-overstate counts; serving-time block and visibility checks; invalidation within a minute; hot-post replication; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Must the count be exact?
clarifications.a: It must never overstate. It may be capped in display (for example "99+ friends") and may briefly understate.

clarifications.q: Which reactions count?
clarifications.a: Reactions and comments, not shares.

clarifications.q: Can I precompute per viewer?
clarifications.a: Yes, if you account for the storage and the freshness.

clarifications.q: What about very old posts?
clarifications.a: Social context matters most in the first days of a post; older posts can be cheaper.

hints: There are two sides: a viewer with hundreds of friends and a post with up to millions of reactors. Iterate over the smaller side and probe the larger one.
Before choosing fan-out on write, compute how many writes it implies per day: reactions times the reactor's friends.
Probes into a very large reactor set can be screened cheaply (for example with a membership filter) and then confirmed.
followups: What is the write amplification of pushing every reaction to every friend's index at {{daily_reactions}} reactions a day and {{avg_friends}} friends, and what happens when someone with 5,000 friends reacts to 300 posts in an hour?
For read-time intersection, how is a post's reactor set laid out so that probing {{avg_friends}} friends against {{top_reactions}} reactors fits in {{latency}}?
A feed page shows 20 posts. How many probes is that per page, and how do you batch them?
How does an un-react reach the viewer's feed within a minute in each design?
Which two friends do you name, and where is that decided so it stays within budget?

rules.ask: How many index writes per day is that at {{daily_reactions}} reactions and {{avg_friends}} friends per reactor, and who pays when one person with 5,000 friends reacts to hundreds of posts?
For a post with {{top_reactions}} reactions, which side do you iterate over, and how many lookups does one render cost?
A false positive would name someone who did not react. What confirms a hit, and what false-positive rate do you choose?
A friend un-reacts. The cached social context still names them. What invalidates it within one minute?
The viewer blocks one of the counted friends. How does your count avoid overstating?

incidents: The reactor set of a post collecting {{top_reactions}} reactions lives on one storage shard. Render traffic for that post saturates the shard, and social context times out for 30% of feed renders in one region.
A person blocks someone. For 20 minutes the blocked person's name still appears under posts in the feed, because social context was cached per viewer and post.
After a major sports final, the fan-out queue is three hours behind. Friends' reactions are missing from social context and counts lag far behind.

templates.title: Moving messaging telemetry in-region before a residency deadline
templates.subtopic: regulatory-deadline migration, influence without authority

scope: people in two regions whose rules differ

sections.scenario: You lead data engineering for the reliability telemetry of a messaging app: delivery metadata, client crash and performance reports, and server health data. A new data-residency requirement means that telemetry about {{scope}} must be stored and processed in-region within {{months}} months. Today everything flows to central storage, and {{pipelines}} pipelines owned by {{teams}} teams read it. The privacy and legal teams have defined what the requirement means; your job is the technical plan and its delivery. Product teams fear losing the global dashboards they rely on during incidents.
sections.problem: How would you lead this: the first weeks, the plan, and delivery to the deadline? Cover how you establish what has to move, the architecture you propose (what stays in-region and what may cross), sequencing and verification, how you get {{teams}} teams to do work they did not plan for, how you manage the risk of missing the date, and how incident response keeps working throughout. Then describe a real migration you led with an external or fixed deadline, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: You do not interpret the requirement; privacy and legal do, and they have said that aggregates meeting a minimum group size may leave the region while anything carrying account or device identifiers may not. Reliability alerting must keep working throughout. The date does not move.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Inventory and classification before planning; scope reduced by retiring unused pipelines; an architecture where identifiable data stays in-region and only qualifying aggregates (mergeable, above the minimum group size) cross; staged migration with verification evidence; incident tooling kept working; cross-team plan with owners, milestones and early warnings; honest status and explicit trade-offs as the date nears; real example with measurable outcome and personal contribution, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Are all the pipelines still used?
clarifications.a: You do not know; some probably are not.

clarifications.q: Is there budget?
clarifications.a: Infrastructure budget for regional capacity, yes. No new team.

clarifications.q: Who owns the deadline?
clarifications.a: A program sponsor in engineering leadership, who expects a monthly status from you.

clarifications.q: Do other teams have to help?
clarifications.a: They own their pipelines; you cannot change them without them.

hints: Inventory and classify first: which pipelines read identifiable data, which read only aggregates, which nobody uses.
The date is fixed; the scope is not. Retiring a pipeline is the cheapest migration.
Compliance is shown with evidence (data-flow tests, storage locations, access logs), not asserted.
followups: Halfway through, a team that owns a third of the pipelines says it cannot start for three months. What do you do?
Global incident dashboards need a p95 delivery latency across all regions. How do you provide it without moving identifiable data?
How do you prove to the privacy team that nothing identifiable leaves the region, including backups and ad hoc extracts?
Four weeks before the date you are 70% done. What do you tell whom, and what are your options?
In your real example, what did you personally decide, and what would you do differently?

rules.ask: A replicated copy outside the region is exactly what the requirement rules out. How do you find every copy, including backups and extracts?
A federated query that returns rows to a central engine moves data. What exactly leaves the region in your design?
You will not finish everything by the date. What do you cut, who agrees to it, and what is the fallback for what remains?
What do you try before escalating, and what does your escalation ask for specifically?
What did you personally decide or do?

templates.title: Ads reporting on-call is burning the team out
templates.subtopic: operational load versus roadmap, advertiser impact

leaving: two engineers have asked to move teams
one senior engineer has resigned, citing on-call
the team's last two hiring candidates declined after hearing about on-call

sections.scenario: Your team of {{team}} engineers owns the pipelines that produce advertisers' daily performance reports: impressions, clicks, spend and attributed conversions by campaign. On-call receives about {{pages}} pages a week, many at night, and last month the reports were late on {{late_days}} days, which produced advertiser support tickets. Meanwhile {{leaving}}. Your director has committed the team to two new reporting features this half. You have just taken over as the team's technical lead.
sections.problem: What do you do in your first month and your first half? Cover how you find out where the load comes from, how you decide what to fix first, how you make the case for reliability work against the committed roadmap, how you look after the people on the team, and how you will know it worked. Then tell me about a real time you reduced operational load or reliability debt while still delivering, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: Advertisers' reports must stay correct; making them late is not a free option. The director's commitments were made publicly inside the organisation. You cannot hire in the next quarter.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Measures the load before acting (pages categorised by cause and actionability); quick wins that remove noise without losing real signal; root-cause fixes ranked by pages and advertiser impact; a negotiated, explicit capacity split with the director, backed by data; upstream dependencies handled with agreements and defensive design; care for people (rotation fairness, recovery time, honest conversations) alongside fixes; measurable targets; real example with personal contribution and outcome, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Are the pages real problems?
clarifications.a: You do not know; nobody has categorised them.

clarifications.q: Why are reports late?
clarifications.a: Mostly upstream data arriving late and jobs being rerun by hand, as far as anyone remembers.

clarifications.q: Does the director know about the attrition?
clarifications.a: They know people are unhappy; they have not seen numbers.

clarifications.q: Do other teams page you for their problems?
clarifications.a: Some alerts fire on upstream delays your team cannot fix.

hints: Data first: categorise a month of pages by cause, action taken and whether action was needed.
Separate alerts that need a human now from those that can wait for morning, and those that belong to another team.
Express the cost of the load in terms the director weighs: late reports, support tickets, delivery speed, attrition.
followups: What do your first two weeks look like, concretely?
The director says the features cannot slip. How do you negotiate capacity for reliability work?
Half the pages come from an upstream team's late data. What do you do about alerts you cannot fix yourself?
What would you measure monthly to show the work is paying off, and what targets would you set?
In your real example, what did you personally change, and what did it cost?

rules.ask: A rebuild takes two quarters while the pages continue. What do you do for the team in the meantime?
Which alerts would you delete, and how do you make sure a real failure still reaches someone?
A better rotation spreads the pain. What actually reduces it?
The upstream team has its own roadmap. What do you ask them for, and what do you build on your side if they say no?
What did you personally decide or do?

templates.title: Changing what counts as a feed impression
templates.subtopic: metric definitions, migration of goals and experiments

change: from 'any part of the post drawn on screen' to 'at least half of the post visible for at least one second'
from 'post sent to the device' to 'post actually visible on screen'

sections.scenario: You lead the logging and metrics platform for a social app's feed. Ranking researchers show that the current impression definition counts posts people scroll past too quickly to see, which adds noise to ranking training data and inflates reach. They propose changing the definition {{change}}. Under the new rule, impressions fall by about {{shift}} and every per-impression rate rises. {{teams}} teams have goals, dashboards and experiments built on the current definition. The change covers organic feed metrics only; ads measurement follows its own published definitions and is out of scope.
sections.problem: How would you lead this change: the evidence you need, who decides, how you migrate goals, dashboards, history and experiments in flight, and how you bring the teams along? Then describe a real time you changed a widely used definition, interface or contract that other teams depended on, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: Experiments in flight cannot be stopped. This quarter's goals are already set. Logging both definitions doubles a significant logging cost, so dual logging must end.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Evidence that the new rule measures attention better (correlation with later actions or surveys, not only ranking gains); clear decision rights; an explicit migration plan with a dual period that ends, rebased goals and a rule for experiments in flight; honest history handling with labelled breaks; communication and support for affected teams; real example with measurable outcome and personal contribution, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Who owns metric definitions?
clarifications.a: A metrics review group with product and data science leads. You bring the proposal; they decide.

clarifications.q: Can the new definition be backfilled?
clarifications.a: Partly. The visibility data the new rule needs has only been logged for the last 30 days.

clarifications.q: Do all teams oppose it?
clarifications.a: No. Some teams' goals look better under the new rule and some look worse.

clarifications.q: Is the new rule known to be better?
clarifications.a: The researchers have evidence for ranking; nobody has checked it against other uses yet.

hints: "Different" is not "better". Decide what evidence would show the new rule measures attention more faithfully.
A definition change moves goals without any change in user experience. Rebase targets explicitly.
Experiments compare arms under one definition. Decide which definition decides each experiment in flight.
followups: A team whose goal metric drops under the new rule asks to delay until next half. What do you do?
Which definition decides experiments that started before the change and end after it?
History: restate with what you can backfill, splice the two series, or start fresh? What does each do to year-over-year charts?
How would you validate that the new definition is better rather than merely different?
In your real example, how did you handle the teams that lost out from the change?

rules.ask: You have only 30 days of visibility data. What do charts that span a year show?
How long do you run both, what does it cost, and what ends it?
One team's goal now looks {{shift}} better with no change in user experience. What happens to their target?
You do not own the other teams' roadmaps. What makes them migrate on time?
Where did you personally disagree, and what did you do about it?

templates.title: The lift result everyone celebrated was wrong
templates.subtopic: correcting a published measurement, process change

flaw: conversions arriving from both the browser and the server were deduplicated in the holdout group but not in the test group
the analysis kept only people who were actually shown an ad in the test group but kept everyone in the holdout group
group assignment used a hash that correlated with account age, so the test group was older on average
audience: a launch review for a new ad format
a case study already shared with advertisers

sections.scenario: Your team runs the measurement pipeline for randomised conversion lift studies, where a holdout group is not shown an advertiser's ads and conversion rates are compared. {{weeks}} weeks ago a study reported a {{lift}} lift, and the result was presented in {{audience}}. You now find that {{flaw}}. Your corrected analysis shows a much smaller lift, with a confidence interval that includes zero. A senior leader championed the original result.
sections.problem: What do you do in the first day and the following weeks? Cover how you confirm the flaw, who you tell and how, how you find other studies with the same problem, how you present a corrected result that is itself uncertain, and what you change so it cannot happen again. Then describe a real time you had to report that your own team's earlier result or number was wrong, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: External communication to advertisers is owned by other teams. Other studies may share the flaw. You cannot rerun the original study with the same timing.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Confirms the flaw quickly with a second reviewer; escalates promptly to the people making decisions, with known, unknown and next update; does not wait for convenient timing; finds and prioritises other affected studies; presents the corrected result with honest uncertainty; owns their part; prevention through automatic checks (sample ratio, covariate balance, identical processing in both groups, A/A tests); real example with personal contribution and outcome, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Are you sure of the flaw?
clarifications.a: Fairly sure; you have reproduced it on one study. Nobody else has reviewed it yet.

clarifications.q: How many other studies used the same pipeline version?
clarifications.a: You do not know yet.

clarifications.q: Is anyone deciding anything on the number now?
clarifications.a: Yes. Budget and launch decisions are being made with it.

clarifications.q: Who wrote the faulty step?
clarifications.a: An engineer on your team, following a review that you approved.

hints: Get a second person to confirm the flaw quickly; then the clock is about decisions being made on a wrong number.
Say what is known, what is not, and when you will know more. A correction that overstates its own certainty repeats the mistake.
The best prevention is a check that runs automatically on every study, not a reminder.
followups: Your manager suggests waiting for the next study to confirm before telling anyone. What do you do?
How do you find every other study affected, and in what order do you correct them?
How do you present a corrected result whose interval includes zero, to an audience that wants a yes or no?
Which automatic checks would have caught this flaw, and where in the pipeline do they run?
In your real example, what did you personally say, to whom, and what happened next?

rules.ask: Budget decisions are being made on the number this week. What is the cost of waiting a month, and who bears it?
What exactly does the correction say, who sends it, and what does it say about the remaining uncertainty?
Which check would have caught this specific flaw, and why was it not there?
You approved the review. How do you keep the follow-up blameless and still own your part?
What did you personally decide or do?

templates.title: Several apps, several definitions of an active person
templates.subtopic: shared metrics layer, consolidation without a mandate

sections.scenario: A company runs several social and messaging apps. Years ago each app built its own daily-active pipeline with its own definition (opened the app; any logged event; sent or received a message) and its own day boundary. There are now {{pipelines}} such pipelines costing about {{cost}} a year combined. The company-wide report of active people differs from the apps' own reports by {{gap}}, and every review starts with an argument about whose number is right. A vice president asks you to propose and deliver a shared metrics layer within {{months}} months. App teams are not required to adopt it.
sections.problem: How would you decide the architecture (one central pipeline, shared definitions over each app's pipeline, a semantic layer, or a hybrid), bring the app teams along, migrate without breaking their goals and reports, and show it worked? Then describe a real consolidation, platform migration or shared-standard effort you led or strongly influenced, with the outcome, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: App teams keep shipping throughout. Some differences between apps are legitimate and some are accidents. A person is counted once across apps only where their accounts are linked under the platform's privacy rules and their own settings; you may not link accounts yourself to improve the count.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Diagnoses differences with evidence and classifies them; compares architectures on explicit criteria (consistency, ownership, cost, migration risk); proposes a staged path with a parallel run and reconciliation; respects privacy rules on cross-app counting with an estimated, labelled figure where accounts are not linked; earns adoption with value for app teams rather than mandate alone; defines success measures (one agreed number, fewer reconciliation disputes, cost); real example with measurable outcome and personal contribution, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Which differences are accidents?
clarifications.a: You do not know yet; some teams use UTC days and others local days, and test accounts are excluded inconsistently.

clarifications.q: Who consumes the numbers?
clarifications.a: Company-wide reports, every app's goals, and many dashboards.

clarifications.q: Is there budget for a new team?
clarifications.a: A small one. Most of the work must come from existing teams.

clarifications.q: Does the largest app want this?
clarifications.a: Not especially. Its pipeline works and it sees cost without benefit.

hints: Separate definitions, code and data: you can share any one of them without sharing the others.
Classify every difference as legitimate or accidental with evidence before proposing anything.
A migration that only creates work for the biggest team will stall. Find what they get out of it.
followups: The largest app team refuses to migrate. What do you do?
What exactly do you centralise: the definition, the code, the data, or the serving layer? Why?
During a parallel run, the new layer and one app's pipeline differ by 3%. Who is right, and how do you find out?
The new layer costs more than the old pipelines for its first two quarters. How do you justify it, and what do you cut?
In your real example, what did you get wrong at first, and how did you change course?

rules.ask: Your team now owns every app's most important metric. What happens to your on-call load and to their release speed?
The same definition applied to different raw logs still gives different numbers. Where does the definition stop and the logging start?
There is no mandate. Why would the largest app adopt in the next {{months}} months?
Many people have not linked their accounts across apps. How do you count them once without linking them yourself, and how do you label that number?
Where did you personally disagree, and what did you do about it?
